name: Unraster
tagline: Browser-based AI background remover aimed at product photos, with a free tier and nothing to install.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Background removal is one of the few AI tasks where the open weights are genuinely competitive with the paid products: RMBG-1.4 and BiRefNet will cut a product photo off a white or cluttered backdrop about as cleanly as a hosted tool does. Transformers.js runs those models in the browser on WebGPU, so a one-shot build is a static page with a drag-and-drop zone, a queue, and a ZIP export, no server and no per-image credits. The gap is not accuracy, it is the long tail: wispy hair, glass, fine mesh, and the matting refinement pass that polished tools quietly layer on top. For e-commerce cutouts of solid objects, which is the stated use case, the DIY version is fine on day one. The main cost is the one-time model download and a browser new enough to have WebGPU.
coreLoopDIY: Drops images onto a local static page, runs a segmentation model fully client-side, and hands back transparent PNGs individually or as a ZIP.
requirements: A browser with WebGPU (recent Chrome or Edge) for usable speed; wasm fallback is slow
A one-time model download of roughly 50 to 180 MB, cached by the browser
Node 20 plus for the dev server and build
No API keys, no account, no backend
whatYouLose: Edge refinement on hair, fur, glass, and transparent packaging, where the paid tools usually win
Fast batch throughput on hundreds of images: your laptop GPU is the bottleneck now
Any API or integration for piping cutouts into a store or pipeline
Shadow regeneration, auto-cropping, and the other post-cutout niceties polished tools bundle
Model upgrades handled for you; you now pin and swap ONNX weights by hand
moatNotes: Whatever matting and refinement stack sits on top of the base segmentation is the actual product; the raw mask is commodity.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because most people buying a background remover are not optimizing for cost, they are optimizing for not thinking about it. A hosted page that works on a phone, handles a 200-image batch without melting the laptop, and cleans up hair edges without a second pass is worth real money to someone shipping a catalog this week. The DIY build is strictly better on privacy and marginal cost and strictly worse on the fiddly 5 percent of images that need actual matting.
notes: The model is free, the mask is free, the last 5 percent of edge quality is the thing you are actually buying.
prompt:
Build a local, fully client-side background remover as a static web app. No backend, no accounts, no telemetry, no analytics, no network calls except fetching model weights from the Hugging Face CDN on first run.

Stack, non-negotiable: Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind. Use @huggingface/transformers (transformers.js v3) for inference. No other heavy deps.

Model: load briaai/RMBG-1.4 via the image-segmentation pipeline, device 'webgpu', dtype 'fp32', with automatic fallback to 'wasm' if WebGPU is unavailable. Download the model inside a web worker so the UI never blocks. Show a progress bar driven by the progress_callback, and tell the user the one-time download size.

UI, one page:
- A large drag-and-drop zone that also accepts a file picker and clipboard paste. Accept jpg, png, webp. Allow many files at once.
- A queue list showing each file with a thumbnail and status: queued, processing, done, failed.
- Process files sequentially through the worker so memory stays bounded. Downscale the longest side to 2048 px before inference, then composite the resulting alpha mask back onto the ORIGINAL full-resolution pixels so output keeps native resolution.
- Result view: before/after with a checkerboard transparency backdrop and a drag slider.
- Per-image download as PNG, plus a 'Download all as ZIP' button using client-side zipping (fflate).
- A background option toggle: transparent, solid white, or a hex color picker, applied at export time only.
- A 'Clear all' button that revokes every object URL.

Explicitly out of scope: shadow generation, auto-crop, upscaling, a hosted API, user accounts, saved history, mobile-native builds.

Quality details that matter: feather the mask by 1 px to avoid jagged edges, keep EXIF orientation correct on input, and never upload a file anywhere.

Include a README with run instructions, the model license note (RMBG-1.4 is non-commercial; state this clearly and mention swapping in BiRefNet or isnet-general if commercial use is needed), and a short section on where edge quality will disappoint: hair, fur, glass, and mesh.

No .env is needed. If you add one later for an optional model mirror, document it and keep it out of git.
